name: FPV newbie FAQ
credit: FPV community FAQs: Oscar Liang (oscarliang.com), Betaflight docs, GetFPV, Rotor Riot, BetaFPV, NewBeeDrone, FPV Know-It-All, IntoFPV, FAA
about: Curated beginner FPV Q&A in original wording, each answer synthesized from and credited to a public source. Built/installed with: python build_faq_pack.py. Keywords are compound/brand-anchored on purpose - bare words like 'battery', 'throttle', 'esc', 'sim' or 'msp' would steal IT questions (laptop battery, bandwidth throttling, escalate, phishing simulator, managed service provider).

faqs.q: What voltage should I charge my LiPo battery to?
faqs.a: A standard LiPo cell is fully charged at 4.20V. LiHV (high-voltage) cells can go to 4.35V per cell, but only if the pack is explicitly rated LiHV. Most chargers let you select the end voltage, so double-check it matches your battery type before charging.

faqs.q: What's the difference between LiPo and LiHV batteries?
faqs.a: LiHV batteries can be charged up to 4.35V per cell instead of the standard 4.20V, making them more energy-dense and giving more punch in the first half of the discharge. LiHV is the popular choice for small 1S tiny whoop packs (300-450mAh), while regular LiPo remains preferred for bigger, higher-cell-count packs.

faqs.q: Can I charge a normal LiPo to 4.35V like a LiHV?
faqs.a: No. Overcharging a standard LiPo to 4.35V can result in a fire. Only charge to 4.35V if the battery is specifically rated as LiHV; standard LiPo must stop at 4.20V per cell.

faqs.q: What is storage voltage and when should I use it?
faqs.a: Storage voltage is 3.80-3.85V per cell, which is roughly 40-50% charge and the most stable, safest state for a LiPo. If you won't fly a battery for more than about 2 weeks, storage-charge it and keep it at room temperature. Batteries ship from the factory at this voltage for a reason.

faqs.q: How low can I let my battery get before landing?
faqs.a: Land at around 3.5V per cell - below that, voltage drops off a cliff and you risk damaging the pack. Never discharge below roughly 3.0-3.3V per cell, as that causes irreversible damage. Set your OSD or battery alarm to warn at 3.5V.

faqs.q: Why does over-discharging hurt my LiPo?
faqs.a: Discharging a LiPo cell below 3.0V causes irreversible performance degradation or outright battery damage, and chargers may refuse to recognize a heavily over-discharged pack. It's generally recommended to stop flying and land around 3.5V per cell to prolong battery lifespan.

faqs.q: What does the mAh number on a battery mean?
faqs.a: mAh is capacity: a 1300mAh battery can supply 1.3A continuously for one hour before it's empty. More mAh means longer flight time but also more weight, which is why tiny whoops stick to small 300-450mAh packs.

faqs.q: What does the C rating mean and how do I calculate max current?
faqs.a: The C rating indicates how much current a battery can safely deliver: Maximum Current Draw = Capacity x C-Rating. For example, a 1500mAh (1.5Ah) 100C pack can theoretically deliver 150A continuous. For a 1S 300mAh 80C whoop pack, that's 24A.

faqs.q: Can I trust the C rating printed on the battery?
faqs.a: Not really. Manufacturer C ratings are often inflated for marketing and have become largely meaningless over the years. Real-world voltage sag under load matters more, so rely on independent testing and brand reputation (e.g. BetaFPV Lava II and NewBeeDrone Nitro Nectar test well for 1S whoop packs).

faqs.q: What batteries should I buy for my tiny whoop?
faqs.a: 1S LiHV packs: 300mAh is the standard for 65mm whoops, and 300-450mAh for 75mm whoops (450mAh gives longer flights at the cost of 4-5g extra weight). Well-tested options include the BetaFPV Lava II 1S 320mAh/480mAh and NewBeeDrone Nitro Nectar 300mAh. Match the connector (BT2.0, PH2.0, GNB27, A30) to your drone.

faqs.q: What's the deal with all the 1S battery connectors (PH2.0, BT2.0, GNB27, A30)?
faqs.a: PH2.0 is the legacy connector and has higher resistance, causing more voltage sag under load. Newer connectors - BT2.0 (BetaFPV), GNB27 (Flywoo/Sub250), A30 (GNB), and NX69 (NewBeeDrone) - handle current better. They are not interchangeable, so buy batteries and a charger that match your whoop's connector.

faqs.q: How fast should I charge my LiPo batteries? What amps do I set?
faqs.a: Charge at 1C or lower: set the charge current equal to the battery capacity. A 1500mAh pack charges at 1.5A; a 1S 300mAh whoop pack at 0.3A (many pilots use up to 0.5A on quality packs). Always balance-charge multi-cell packs and never leave charging batteries unattended.

faqs.q: What charger do I need for 1S whoop batteries?
faqs.a: Get a dedicated multi-port 1S LiPo/LiHV charger such as the VIFLY WhoopStor V3, BetaFPV HexaCharger Pro, or GEPRC WooPower. The WhoopStor V3 has 6 independent ports with both BT2.0 and PH2.0 connectors, selectable end voltage (3.80V, 3.85V, 4.20V LiPo, or 4.35V LiHV), and adjustable current from 0.3A to 1.3A.

faqs.q: Can I power a 1S whoop charger from any USB port?
faqs.a: Usually not a plain 5V port. The VIFLY WhoopStor V3 requires USB-C PD (9-20V), an XT60 input from a 2S-6S battery, or a DC barrel jack - regular 5V USB is not supported. Similarly, the Flywoo EasyPower E16 needs a USB-C PD source with at least 45W. Check your charger's input requirements and use a proper PD wall adapter.

faqs.q: How long does it take to charge a whoop battery?
faqs.a: Roughly 20 minutes: the BetaFPV HexaCharger Pro takes about 20 minutes on average to charge a 1S 300mAh LiHV pack from 3.3V to 4.35V at 1A. With a 6-port charger you can rotate packs and fly nearly continuously.

faqs.q: How long does a tiny whoop fly on one battery?
faqs.a: Typically 2-4 minutes depending on how hard you fly. For example, the BetaFPV Air65 manages about 4:00-4:30 on a 1S 300mAh pack even with aggressive flying at 50-60% throttle. Heavier whoops and harder flying mean shorter flights.

faqs.q: My battery is puffed or swollen - can I still use it?
faqs.a: No. Once a LiPo becomes swollen the damage is irreversible, and you should dispose of it properly as soon as possible. Never puncture a LiPo, as that can cause a fire. Store it somewhere fireproof until you can take it to a battery recycling point.

faqs.q: How do I safely dispose of an old LiPo battery?
faqs.a: Discharge it completely first - a halogen light bulb discharger or power resistor works well (smart charger discharge functions usually cut off around 3.0V, which isn't low enough). Once fully drained, cut off the connector, strip and twist the leads together, then take it to a battery recycling facility. Never throw LiPos in the trash or puncture them.

faqs.q: Should I use the salt water method to dispose of LiPos?
faqs.a: It's not the best method. Salt water discharges the battery very slowly (two weeks or more), often incompletely, and corrosion on the connectors can stop the discharge entirely. Its only advantage is safety from full immersion; a light bulb or resistor discharge followed by recycling is faster and more reliable.

faqs.q: How should I store my LiPo batteries between sessions?
faqs.a: If you won't fly for more than about 2 weeks, bring packs to storage voltage (3.80-3.85V per cell) - many 1S chargers like the WhoopStor V3 have a storage mode that charges or discharges packs to that level automatically. Store at room temperature in a fireproof container like a LiPo bag, away from flammables.

faqs.q: When I'm landing my whoop, what voltage should the battery alarm be set to?
faqs.a: NewBeeDrone recommends setting the low-voltage warning at 3.5V and bringing the whoop in to land by 3.3V; flying below 3.3V degrades the battery. Note these are under-load readings - the resting voltage after landing will bounce back somewhat higher.

faqs.q: Should I buy an all-in-one RTF kit like the BetaFPV Cetus, or separate gear?
faqs.a: RTF (ready-to-fly) kits like the BetaFPV Cetus bundle a whoop, a basic radio, and basic goggles for the cheapest possible entry, and they work. The common community caveat - and the reason many get returned or outgrown fast - is that the bundled radio and goggles are entry-grade and locked to the kit's ecosystem, so most of the kit gets replaced once you're hooked (the base Cetus also uses brushed motors, which wear out; the Cetus Pro is brushless). The widely repeated alternative: a real radio (Radiomaster Pocket or Boxer), a standalone BNF whoop (Air65 or Mobula6), and budget goggles - more up front, but nothing gets thrown away.

faqs.q: What exactly is a tiny whoop?
faqs.a: A tiny whoop is a small FPV drone with protective propeller ducts, designed to be flown indoors and around people safely. They come mainly in 65mm and 75mm motor-to-motor sizes, run on 1S batteries, and weigh only about 17-24g dry, so crashes rarely damage anything.

faqs.q: Should I get a 65mm or 75mm whoop?
faqs.a: 65mm whoops (31mm props, ~18-20g) are lighter and more agile - ideal for indoor flying in tight spaces. 75mm whoops (40mm props, ~20-24g) have more power, longer flight times, and handle outdoor flying on calm days better, but are more challenging indoors. If you'll mostly fly inside your house, start with 65mm.

faqs.q: What's the best first tiny whoop to buy?
faqs.a: The BetaFPV Air65 (~17g, ExpressLRS, 400mW analog VTX) is rated the best value-for-performance 65mm whoop; the Happymodel Mobula6 2024 is a close alternative. The NewBeeDrone Hummingbird V4 is beginner-friendly thanks to durability and strong customer support, and the BetaFPV Air75 (~$95) suits outdoor-leaning pilots. For digital HD video, look at the BetaFPV Meteor75 Pro O4.

faqs.q: Why is the BetaFPV Air65 so recommended?
faqs.a: It weighs only about 17.25g without battery yet flies 4+ minutes on a 1S 300mAh pack, comes with a built-in ExpressLRS receiver and 400mW analog VTX, and has better quality control than most competitors while costing about $20 less than the Mobula6 2024. Main beginner gripe: even the lowest camera angle is a bit high for slow indoor flying.

faqs.q: Is the Happymodel Mobula6 2024 a good beginner whoop?
faqs.a: Yes - Oscar Liang's review calls it possibly the best BNF tiny whoop of its year. It weighs just 17.7g, uses SE0702 brushless motors with an ELRS receiver and OpenVTX on an all-in-one board, and the 2024 frame adds a raised lip protecting the camera. Motors connect via plugs, so repairs need no soldering.

faqs.q: Should I start with a tiny whoop or a 5-inch drone?
faqs.a: Tiny whoops are safer, cheaper to repair, and let you practice indoors year-round, while 5-inch quads develop your skills faster if you have open outdoor space - Oscar Liang says if you're serious about developing FPV skills, a 5-inch is the better long-term trainer. Many pilots do both: whoop indoors, 5-inch outdoors. Either way, put in simulator hours first.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to get into FPV?
faqs.a: Expect roughly $400-$1,800 total: radio controller plus simulator $100-$300, FPV goggles $100-$500, the drone itself $100-$500, and batteries/charger/tools another $100-$500. Starting with a tiny whoop and budget analog goggles keeps you at the low end.

faqs.q: Brushed or brushless motors for a whoop?
faqs.a: Brushless, no question - Oscar Liang calls it 'a no brainer.' Brushless whoops support turtle mode, higher PWM frequencies, and RPM filtering, and brushed whoops are effectively obsolete since brushed motors wear out quickly.

faqs.q: What accessories do I need with my first tiny whoop?
faqs.a: A proper 1S multi-port charger (e.g. VIFLY WhoopStor V3), several spare batteries, a propeller removal tool, and spare props and frame parts. A circular-polarized antenna upgrade for your goggles helps video quality too. Budget for these up front - one battery means two-minute sessions.

faqs.q: What radio transmitter should I buy as a beginner?
faqs.a: The Radiomaster Pocket (~$65) is the go-to beginner pick: it runs EdgeTX with ExpressLRS built in, though it has smaller gimbals and limited RF power. The Radiomaster T8L (~$35) is the ultra-budget option, and the Radiomaster Boxer is the best value step-up, offering most of the flagship TX16S features for much less. All work with simulators over USB.

faqs.q: Why does everyone recommend ExpressLRS (ELRS)?
faqs.a: ExpressLRS is currently the most popular FPV radio link thanks to its affordability, high performance, open-source nature, and cutting-edge features. Your radio choice locks you into a receiver ecosystem (you need a matching receiver in every drone), so picking ELRS 2.4GHz gives you the widest selection of whoops and parts.

faqs.q: What is an ExpressLRS binding phrase?
faqs.a: A binding phrase is a text passphrase that tells every ELRS transmitter and receiver you own 'we belong together' - any receiver flashed with the same phrase binds automatically. It's optional but strongly recommended (use at least 8 unique alphanumeric characters so you don't collide with other pilots). You can set it when flashing firmware or via the receiver's WiFi web UI on v3.0+.

faqs.q: How do I bind an ELRS receiver without a binding phrase?
faqs.a: Use the three power cycle method: plug in and unplug the battery (or USB) three times quickly; on the third power-up the receiver LED double-flashes, indicating bind mode. Then open the ExpressLRS Lua script on your radio and select Bind. A solid LED confirms a successful bind.

faqs.q: How do I set a bind phrase over WiFi on an ELRS receiver?
faqs.a: On firmware v3+, power the receiver and wait for it to enter WiFi mode (fast-flashing LED), connect your computer/phone to the 'ExpressLRS RX' hotspot with password 'expresslrs', browse to 10.0.0.1, and enter your binding phrase in the web UI. This is also the easiest way to fix a receiver that's bound to someone else's phrase.

faqs.q: My ELRS receiver won't bind - what's wrong?
faqs.a: The most common cause is a firmware version mismatch: the major version of transmitter and receiver must match (both on v3, for example) - minor version differences are fine. Otherwise, the receiver may already hold a different bind phrase; re-flash it or update the phrase via the WiFi web UI.

faqs.q: What do the ELRS receiver LED patterns mean?
faqs.a: Double-flash means bind mode is active, fast flashing means WiFi mode is active, and a solid LED means the receiver is bound and connected to your transmitter. Slow blinking generally means it's waiting for a connection.

faqs.q: What is Mode 2 on a radio?
faqs.a: Mode 2 puts throttle and yaw on the left stick and pitch and roll on the right stick. It's the standard for FPV in most of the world - buy your radio in Mode 2 unless you have a strong reason not to, so tutorials and simulators match your muscle memory.

faqs.q: Do I need hall sensor gimbals on my first radio?
faqs.a: Hall sensor gimbals are contactless and more durable than potentiometer gimbals, which wear out faster due to physical contacts. That said, either type will likely outlast your flying career, so don't let gimbal type alone drive your first purchase.

faqs.q: What is Betaflight and how do I connect to it?
faqs.a: Betaflight is the open-source flight control firmware most FPV drones run, configured through the Betaflight Configurator - use the web app at https://app.betaflight.com in Chrome. Connect the flight controller over a USB data cable, and check the Setup tab: the 3D model should move exactly as you tilt the drone.

faqs.q: How do I arm my drone in Betaflight?
faqs.a: Arming is done with a switch: assign a radio switch to channel 5-12, then in the Modes tab click Add Range on ARM and set the range your switch activates. Before it will arm, throttle must be at minimum and the quad must be level. When armed the props spin at idle - always arm with the quad on the ground, away from you.

faqs.q: My quad won't arm - how do I find out why?
faqs.a: Betaflight encodes every blocker as an 'arming disable flag.' Check it three ways: type 'status' in the CLI (flags are on the last line), look at the Arming Disable Flags field in the Configurator Setup tab, or enable the arming-disabled warning in your OSD. Fix every listed flag and the quad will arm.

faqs.q: What does the MSP arming flag mean in Betaflight?
faqs.a: MSP means the flight controller thinks a computer is connected, which blocks arming as a safety measure. The fix is simple: unplug the USB cable and close the Betaflight Configurator connection. This is one of the most common 'won't arm' causes for beginners testing on the bench.

faqs.q: What does the ANGLE arming flag mean?
faqs.a: The craft is tilted more than the allowed arming angle - by default it must be level within small_angle, which is 25 degrees. Place the quad on flat ground before arming, or if you intentionally arm on slopes, increase the maximum arm angle setting.

faqs.q: What does the THROTTLE arming flag mean?
faqs.a: Your throttle stick is above the minimum threshold - it must be below min_check (default 1050) to arm. Pull throttle all the way down, and verify in the Receiver tab that your throttle channel actually reads close to 1000 at the bottom; if not, recalibrate your radio endpoints to 1000-2000.

faqs.q: What does the RXLOSS arming flag mean?
faqs.a: The flight controller isn't receiving a valid signal from your receiver. Check that the receiver is bound to your radio and that the channel bars in the Betaflight Receiver tab move when you move the sticks. If they don't, fix binding or the receiver protocol settings (ELRS uses Serial RX with CRSF protocol).

faqs.q: Why won't my quad arm right after plugging in the battery?
faqs.a: Two common reasons: BOOTGRACE means you tried to arm too soon - Betaflight enforces a grace period (pwr_on_arm_grace, default 5 seconds) after power-on. ARMSWITCH means your arm switch was already on when you powered up; toggle it off and on again. Both are safety features, not bugs.

faqs.q: What do the beeps mean when arming fails?
faqs.a: If a beeper is fitted, a failed arm attempt produces five short 'attention' beeps followed by a coded pattern: count (5 x long beeps) + short beeps to get the number of the specific arming-disabled condition in the Betaflight documentation table.

faqs.q: How do I flash or update Betaflight firmware?
faqs.a: Put the flight controller into DFU/bootloader mode by holding the small Boot button while plugging in USB (or type 'bl' in the CLI if the button is buried in the frame), then use the Configurator's Firmware Flasher to select your exact board target and flash. Enable Full Chip Erase when updating to wipe old settings that could conflict - save a CLI diff backup first.

faqs.q: Do I really need to remove props when working in Betaflight?
faqs.a: Yes - always remove all propellers before testing motors or configuring the drone on USB. Motors can spool up unexpectedly (especially with Air Mode or the Motors tab), and spinning props are the most dangerous part of a drone. Also bench-test failsafe: arm (props off), switch off your radio, and confirm motors stop within a couple of seconds.

faqs.q: Which switch arms my BetaFPV bind-and-fly whoop?
faqs.a: BetaFPV BNF drones come configured to arm via channel 5 (AUX1). Assign a two-position switch on your radio to channel 5, then verify in the Betaflight Modes tab that the ARM range matches the values your switch outputs (check live in the Receiver tab).

faqs.q: Why won't my flight controller connect to Betaflight or enter flashing mode?
faqs.a: It's usually a driver problem on Windows. For normal connection the FC uses a VCP/COM port driver; for DFU (flashing) mode it needs a different driver, often fixed with the ImpulseRC Driver Fixer or Zadig. Also make sure you're using a USB data cable, not a charge-only cable - that's a very common gotcha.

faqs.q: What's a good way to find my whoop after crashing out of sight?
faqs.a: Enable the DShot Beacon in Betaflight, which turns your motors into audible beepers you can trigger from a radio switch - no extra hardware needed. Reviewing your goggle DVR footage to see where you went down is the other standard trick.

faqs.q: How do I know which prop goes on which motor?
faqs.a: Quads use two clockwise and two counter-clockwise props on diagonal pairs, and each prop must spin in the same direction as its motor - check the rotation arrows/diagram in the Betaflight Motors tab and the prop's markings or blade pitch. Betaflight's default rotation scheme is 'props in'; mounting a prop backwards or on the wrong motor means the quad flips instantly on takeoff.

faqs.q: How do I remove and replace tiny whoop props?
faqs.a: Whoop props are press-fitted onto the bare motor shaft, and pulling them off by hand puts force on the shaft and bell that can cause 'slip shaft' and ruin the motor. Use a dedicated prop puller - the wire-loop style grabs all blades and pulls straight off the shaft, or the tapered-fork type pushes a pin against the shaft tip. New props simply press back on while you support the motor.

faqs.q: When should I replace my props?
faqs.a: Whenever they're chipped, bent, or the quad starts vibrating or oscillating - damaged props are a major vibration source that hurts tuning and video. Props are the cheapest part of the drone, so keep spares; for 65mm whoops common picks are HQ 31mm Ultralight or Gemfan 1219S, and for 75mm the Gemfan 1610 or HQ 40mm.

faqs.q: What motor size and KV do tiny whoops use?
faqs.a: 65mm whoops use 0702 or 0802 motors in roughly 23,000-30,000KV; 0702 is lighter and preferred for indoor flying, while heavier 0802s suit outdoor use. 75mm whoops use 1002 motors, or 1102 for heavier digital (HD camera) builds. The number format is stator diameter and height in mm (07mm x 02mm).

faqs.q: Does higher KV mean a better whoop motor?
faqs.a: Higher KV (e.g. 26,000KV+) gives more responsiveness and punch but burns battery faster; lower KV (around 23,000KV) gives better efficiency and flight time but feels less powerful in ultra-light builds. 1S whoops need very high KV because a single cell only supplies up to 4.35V - it's a trade-off, not a quality ranking.

faqs.q: A motor spins the wrong direction - do I have to re-solder wires?
faqs.a: No. With modern ESCs you reverse motor direction in software: use the ESC configurator (Bluejay/BLHeli) or the Motor Direction tool in the Betaflight Motors tab, with props removed. Swapping any two of the three motor wires also works but soldering is unnecessary.

faqs.q: Should I get analog or digital (HD) FPV as a beginner?
faqs.a: Analog is the cheapest entry (camera+VTX around $15-40, goggles from $80) with near-zero latency and no ecosystem lock-in, but the picture looks like old standard-definition TV. Digital systems (DJI, Walksnail, HDZero) cost more but give a dramatically better image - Oscar Liang's guidance is 'if you can, get DJI.' For tiny whoops, analog remains popular because it's the lightest and cheapest.

faqs.q: How do the FPV video systems compare on latency and image quality?
faqs.a: Analog and HDZero are lowest latency at roughly 10-20ms glass-to-glass; DJI and Walksnail run about 20-50ms depending on mode and conditions. Image quality: DJI leads (1080p transmission, O4 Pro records 4K), Walksnail is a close second at 1080p/60fps, HDZero is 720p/60 or 540p/90 with very consistent latency (popular with racers), and analog is far behind all of them.

faqs.q: If I buy DJI goggles, can I use them with other video systems?
faqs.a: Mostly no - none of the digital systems are cross-compatible, so once you choose a system you're effectively locked into that ecosystem. DJI goggles only support DJI air units; Walksnail Goggles X and HDZero goggles are more flexible, supporting analog via AV-in and each other via HDMI. Factor this lock-in into your first goggle purchase.

faqs.q: Which video system should I run on a tiny whoop?
faqs.a: Analog is the default for whoops because the VTXs are the lightest and cheapest, and HDZero offers all-in-one flight controller boards for micros. If you want HD on a 65mm whoop, Joshua Bardwell points to the Walksnail Avatar HD Mini 1S Lite kit (about 3g lighter than the regular 1S kit) or the HDZero Eco bundle at 7-8g total; for DJI, buy a prebuilt like the BetaFPV Meteor75 Pro O4.

faqs.q: Box goggles vs binocular goggles - what's the difference?
faqs.a: Box goggles use a single 3-6 inch LCD viewed through a lens: cheaper ($54-$220), roomier (often usable over glasses), with a wide 50-80 degree FOV but lower image quality. Binocular goggles use two small high-quality displays (often OLED), are compact and light, but cost $500-$800 and need IPD/diopter adjustment to fit your eyes. Beginners on a budget usually start with box goggles.

faqs.q: What are good budget FPV goggles for a beginner?
faqs.a: For analog: the BetaFPV VR04 (~$75) has a built-in DVR, upgradable antenna, and channel auto-search, while the Skyzone Cobra SD (~$170) is the best budget box goggle with solid image quality. For digital, the DJI Goggles N3 (~$229) is the cheapest entry into the DJI ecosystem and works with O4 air units.

faqs.q: What is DVR in FPV goggles and do I need it?
faqs.a: DVR records the exact video feed you see in your goggles to a micro SD card, adding no weight to the drone. It's extremely useful for finding crashed drones (scrub the footage to see where you went down) and for reviewing flights, so it's worth prioritizing even in budget goggles.

faqs.q: Do I really need to practice in a simulator before flying?
faqs.a: Yes - Rotor Riot says if they could give only one recommendation it would be to use an FPV simulator first, with at least 5 hours before flying the real thing (Oscar Liang recommends 10+). Sims let you crash hundreds of times for free while building the muscle memory that transfers directly to a real quad, especially if you practice with a real radio.

faqs.q: Which FPV simulator should I get?
faqs.a: Liftoff ($19.99) has the best structured training for beginners; Velocidrone ($19.99) has the most realistic racing physics and hundreds of community tracks; Uncrashed and TRYP FPV ($14.99 each) excel at freestyle with great visuals; DRL Simulator is $9.99 and FPV Freerider is $4.99-$9.99 for low-end PCs. Any of them teaches the fundamentals - pick one and put in hours.

faqs.q: Is there a free FPV simulator?
faqs.a: Yes - FPV SkyDive is free on Windows, macOS, and Linux and is Oscar Liang's pick for best free option. It's a great way to test whether you enjoy FPV before spending anything beyond a radio.

faqs.q: Is there a simulator specifically for tiny whoops?
faqs.a: Yes - Liftoff: Micro Drones ($5.99), made by the Liftoff developers specifically for the tiny whoop class. It simulates 1S micro quads in indoor environments, which matches whoop flying far better than the 5-inch physics of the main sims.

faqs.q: What do I need to run an FPV simulator?
faqs.a: A PC and a real FPV radio connected via USB - power the radio, plug in USB-C, and select USB Joystick mode, then calibrate in the sim's controller settings. Using a proper radio (not a game controller) is important because it builds the exact muscle memory you'll use on a real drone.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Angle, Horizon, and Acro mode?
faqs.a: Angle mode self-levels when you center the sticks and limits maximum tilt - it flies like a camera drone. Horizon mode is Angle with the ability to flip/roll when you push the stick past a threshold. Acro (rate) mode has no self-leveling at all: the sticks command rotation rate and the quad holds whatever attitude you leave it in - it's what virtually all experienced FPV pilots fly.

faqs.q: Should I learn Acro mode or stay in Angle mode?
faqs.a: Learn Acro, ideally from the start in the simulator. Oscar Liang's beginner guide is blunt: self-level modes are tempting, but if you want to get good at FPV it's crucial to learn Acro mode, and relying on auto-level is listed among the top beginner mistakes. Angle mode still has a place for casual indoor whooping in tight spaces.

faqs.q: What is Acro Trainer mode?
faqs.a: Acro Trainer is a Betaflight mode that gives you Acro-style rate control but with a tilt-angle limit that prevents the quad from flipping over and pile-driving into the ground. It's a useful stepping stone: progress from Angle to Acro Trainer, then to full Acro.

faqs.q: What is Air Mode?
faqs.a: Air Mode keeps PID stabilization fully active even at zero throttle, so you keep control authority during dives, flips, and throttle cuts - essential for freestyle. Be careful on the bench: with Air Mode on, motors can spool up unexpectedly while armed on the ground.

faqs.q: What is Turtle mode (flip over after crash)?
faqs.a: Turtle mode spins selected motors in reverse so a crashed, upside-down quad can flip itself back upright - a huge time saver for whoops landing on roofs or behind furniture. It requires DShot ESC protocol and is assigned to a switch in the Betaflight Modes tab.

faqs.q: Why is throttle control so hard, and how do I improve?
faqs.a: In Acro there's no altitude hold, so managing height is entirely on you - it's the most common beginner struggle. Key habit: lower the throttle slowly and smoothly; cutting it abruptly makes the quad free-fall and crash. Hovering practice, figure-8s, and simulator time develop the fine control faster than anything else.

faqs.q: Is it okay to fly my whoop in Angle mode indoors?
faqs.a: Yes - the IntoFPV community consensus is that Angle mode is fine for tight indoor spaces and some experienced whoop pilots fly indoors in Angle permanently. If you want to progress, the suggested path is Angle, then Acro Trainer (which stops you from inverting and slamming into the floor at full throttle), then full Acro. Adding throttle expo helps tame the indoor 'yo-yo' altitude bouncing.

faqs.q: What is prop wash and why does my quad shake when descending?
faqs.a: Prop wash is turbulence from your own propellers disturbing the air the quad then flies through, showing up as oscillations/shaking during fast descents and sharp 180-degree turns. The quad is literally falling through its own dirty air, and the flight controller struggles to stabilize against the chaotic airflow.

faqs.q: How do I reduce prop wash oscillation?
faqs.a: Technique first: pitch forward slightly during descents instead of dropping straight down through your own wake. On the software side, enable RPM filtering (and disable the Gyro Lowpass 1 filter once RPM filtering is on), increase D-term gradually, and enable Dynamic Idle. Also keep hardware clean: undamaged props, tight screws, and a properly soft-mounted flight controller.

faqs.q: Do I need to learn soldering for FPV?
faqs.a: Eventually, yes - soldering is one of the most important FPV skills for repairs like replacing motors, receivers, or battery connectors. The core technique is simple: tin the pads and wires first before joining them, work quickly without rushing, and use flux generously. Some whoops (like the Mobula6 2024) use plug-in motors, which delays the need.

faqs.q: What solder should I buy for drone repairs?
faqs.a: 63/37 leaded solder (63% tin, 37% lead) is the consistent recommendation - it has a short transition between liquid and solid, which helps prevent dry joints, and it flows at lower temperatures than lead-free. Pair it with rosin flux, and clean joints afterwards with isopropyl alcohol.

faqs.q: What temperature should I set my soldering iron to?
faqs.a: With 63/37 solder: about 390C (734F) for signal wires on flight controllers and ESCs, and 450C (842F) for large joints like XT60 connectors and ESC power pads - high heat applied briefly beats low heat applied for ages, which cooks pads. A higher-wattage iron holds its temperature better when it touches the joint.

faqs.q: My solder joint looks dull and grainy - is that bad?
faqs.a: Yes, that's a cold joint, which means bad electrical contact. Fix it by reheating the joint with a bit of flux and adding solder until it turns shiny and smooth. For solder bridges between adjacent pads, remove the excess with solder wick or a desoldering tool.

faqs.q: How do I avoid destroying my flight controller while soldering?
faqs.a: Cover the areas you're not working on with masking, electrical, or Kapton tape - molten solder can spit tiny balls that short components. Hold work steady with helping hands or blu-tack, keep the iron tip clean and tinned, and never solder on a board with a battery connected.

faqs.q: Do I have to register my tiny whoop with the FAA?
faqs.a: Not if you fly recreationally and it weighs under 250g (0.55 lb) including battery - tiny whoops at ~20-30g are far below the limit. Drones 250g and over flown recreationally must be registered at FAADroneZone for $5, valid 3 years. If you fly under Part 107 (commercially), every drone must be registered regardless of weight.

faqs.q: What is the TRUST test and do I need it?
faqs.a: TRUST (The Recreational UAS Safety Test) is required by law for all recreational drone pilots in the US, even for sub-250g whoops. It's free, taken online in about 30 minutes, you can't fail (wrong answers are corrected and re-asked), and you must carry your completion certificate when flying.

faqs.q: Do I need a Part 107 license, or can I fly recreationally?
faqs.a: It depends on intent: if you fly strictly for fun with no direct or indirect compensation, you qualify for the recreational exception (Section 44809) and just need TRUST. Any business purpose - real estate shots, roof inspections, even monetized YouTube videos - makes the flight commercial, requiring a Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate (FAA knowledge test plus TSA background check). When in doubt, assume Part 107 applies.

faqs.q: Does my drone need Remote ID?
faqs.a: Only if it requires registration: since September 16, 2023, any drone that must be registered also has to broadcast Remote ID, unless flown at a FRIA (FAA-Recognized Identification Area). Sub-250g recreational whoops that don't need registration don't need Remote ID either.

faqs.q: Where and how high can I legally fly recreationally in the US?
faqs.a: Keep the drone within visual line of sight (a spotter is required when you're wearing FPV goggles), and fly at or below 400 feet in Class G uncontrolled airspace. In controlled airspace near airports you need prior authorization (e.g. via LAANC). Indoor flying isn't FAA airspace, which is part of why tiny whoops are such a popular starting point.

faqs.q: What are the most common beginner mistakes in FPV?
faqs.a: Per Oscar Liang's beginner guide: skipping simulator practice, buying a radio that doesn't work with sims or future drones, relying on auto-level mode instead of learning Acro, powering on a VTX without checking channels when other pilots are around, and trying to catch a falling drone out of the air (let it crash - props cut). Avoid those five and your first months go much smoother.
